newsitem.title: FRANCE: Strasbourg mayor urges calm at far-right congress.
newsitem.headline: Strasbourg mayor urges calm at far-right congress.

text.p: The mayor of Strasbourg appealed for calm ahead of a weekend congress of France's National Front expected to prompt a big protest demonstration, saying far-right leader Jean-Marie Le Pen's presence could prompt clashes.
Some 20,000 people from across France are expected to take part in demonstrations in the eastern city when the Front holds its annual national congress.

"I have repealtedy appealed for calm...I have written to the Interior Ministry to demand that there be sufficent police forces to assure people's security," Socialist mayor Catherine Trautmann told Europe-1 radio on Thursday.

"Le Pen has decided not to go the cathedral because he said that his presence might cause clashes. That is the first time that Mr Le Pen publicly recognises that he is himself a cause of clashes and that choosing to come to Strasbourg creates problems," Trautmann said.
She has said she cannot legally ban the congress and has called in national police reinforcements to avert feared clashes between anti-fascist demonstrators and hard-right militants.

National Front number two Bruno Megret said violence was very likely because "establishment thugs" were bent on causing trouble. He told a news conference the 2,200 delegates would be asked to remain inside the congress centre to avoid incidents.
Trautmann will lead a march against Le Pen, who has filed a lawsuit against persons unknown for an allegedly conspiracy to disrupt the congress.

The mayor has had a statue of Joan of Arc, the mediaeval heroine who symbolises national independence, removed from its pedestal outside the Alsatian capital's cathedral to prevent Le Pen using it as a rallying point.
"The statue will return once it has been cleaned and once we are certain that it will not be damaged," she said.
Late on Wednesday, several members of the ruling centre-right coalition denounced the Front's stance and also criticised the Left's response at a public rally in Strasbourg.
Jean-Francois Mancel, general secretary of the Gaullist RPR, accused leftist parties of "media-friendly gesticulation". He said the Front was racist and anti-Semitic.
Culture Minister Philippe Douste-Blazy told the rally that the more other politicians attacked the Front, the more its popularity rose in opinion polls.
The centre-right coalition has refused to take part in a demonstration called by local associations and left-wing parties for Saturday afternoon.
"I caution against any violence which the Front congress could spark. That would only benefit the Front which awaits rather than fears them," Douste-Blazy said.
Le Pen has chosen to hold the congress in the region where he won his biggest score in the 1995 presidential election. He polled 25 percent in Alsace compared to 15 percent nationwide.
